title: Smriti Mandhana's India Crush Sri Lanka by 147 Runs to Defend Asian Games Cricket Gold
excerpt: Harmanpreet Kaur's team posted 216/3 and bowled Sri Lanka out for 69 in the Aichi-Nagoya final, securing India's first gold of the Games and back-to-back Asian cricket titles.
body:
• India's women beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the Asian Games 2026 final at Aichi-Nagoya on September 22, posting 216/3 before bowling Sri Lanka out for 69.
  • Smriti Mandhana's 79 off 45 balls led the innings, with a 99-run opening stand alongside Shafali Verma (48) and an unbeaten 49 off 22 from Richa Ghosh.
  • The victory was India's first gold medal of the Games and its second consecutive Asian Games cricket title after Hangzhou.
  • India closed the Games with 85 medals and a clean sweep of all six gold medals across men's and women's cricket, kabaddi, and hockey.

A statement final

The final was over as a contest long before the last ball. Batting first at Aichi-Nagoya, India's women amassed 216 for 3 — then skittled Sri Lanka for 69 in 15.4 overs to win the Asian Games 2026 cricket gold by 147 runs, one of the most comprehensive margins in a major multi-sport final.

https://x.com/Cricketracker/status/2108212915585376718

"The country finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver, 37 bronze — behind China, Japan, and South Korea, below its record 106-medal haul at Hangzhou."

Captain Harmanpreet Kaur's side built the innings on a blazing start. Openers Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma stitched together 99 runs inside the powerplay, attacking from the first over. Mandhana's 79 off 45 balls blended timing with authority, while Shafali's trademark fearlessness produced a 48-ball 48. Wicketkeeper Richa Ghosh finished the assault with an unbeaten 49 off just 22 balls, dragging India past 200 with ease.

The bowling was more ruthless still. Sri Lanka never recovered from the early strikes, crumbling under sustained pressure as Deepti Sharma, Shafali, and the rest of the attack shared the wickets. Sharp fielding turned half-chances into dismissals, and the gulf between the defending champions and the rest of Asia was laid bare.

The road to gold

The campaign had been flawless. India opened with an eight-wicket quarterfinal win over Japan, then hammered Bangladesh by 114 runs in the semifinal — powered by a century from Shafali Verma. The final made it three dominant wins in three outings, and it delivered India's first gold medal of the Aichi-Nagoya Games.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Uqjja5BGX5s

The title defense adds to a remarkable run. India also won the women's cricket gold at Hangzhou, making this back-to-back Asian Games crowns and confirming the depth of the women's program — a squad that has now moved well beyond its senior core.

A golden finish for India

The cricket gold was the headline of a campaign India will remember for its team-sport dominance. The country finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver, 37 bronze — behind China, Japan, and South Korea, below its record 106-medal haul at Hangzhou. But India swept all six gold medals on offer across men's and women's cricket, kabaddi, and hockey.

The men's cricket team added its own gold by beating arch-rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in the final, powered by Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma, and Axar Patel. The women's hockey team ended a 44-year wait by defeating China 1-0 — a win that also booked direct qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Kabaddi delivered both titles: the women edged Iran 37-34, the men came from behind to win 40-34.

What it means

For Indian cricket, the women's dominance at consecutive Asian Games cements their status as the standard-setters in the Asian game. For the diaspora that fills stadiums from New York to Melbourne to watch these players, it was a familiar script: Mandhana and Shafali at the top, power and poise through the middle, and a bowling attack that gave Sri Lanka nowhere to hide. The next horizon is the Olympics — with women's hockey already qualified for LA 2028, cricket's own Olympic return is the milestone this generation is now chasing.
